title: King Horn
description: The earliest surviving Middle English romance, some 1,500 short couplet lines telling the exile, adventures, and restoration of Horn, son of the murdered king of Suddene, who wins the love of Rymenhild, defeats the Saracen invaders, and regains his kingdom. Its spare, ballad-like narrative makes it the classic of the 'ancestral romance' of exile and return.
plot_or_argument: Horn, cast adrift by the invaders who killed his father, grows up at the court of King Aylmar, where Rymenhild loves him; exiled through the envy of Fikenhild, he proves himself in Ireland, rescues Rymenhild from a forced marriage in disguise as a beggar, and returns to avenge his father and reclaim Suddene.
narrative_structure: A tripartite exile-and-return plot with disguise, recognition, and wedding scenes; narrated in terse couplets with abrupt transitions.
principal_characters: Horn; Rymenhild; Fikenhild; King Aylmar; Athulf; the Saracen invaders
meter_and_prosody: Short rhyming couplets, often of three stresses, with formulaic diction.
historical_context: Composed c. 1225 in the south of England from an Anglo-Norman source (the Romance of Horn of Thomas); preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27 (c. 1300) and two later manuscripts.
literary_significance: The fountainhead of the English romance tradition and the earliest witness to the exile-and-return plot that governs the genre.
bibliographical_notes: Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27; Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108; BL Harley MS 2253. Standard edition: in Four Romances of England, TEAMS (1999).

title: Havelok the Dane
alternative_titles: The Lay of Havelok the Dane
description: A Lincolnshire romance of some 3,000 lines on the dispossessed prince Havelok, brought up as a kitchen-boy at Grimsby, whose royal birthmark, strength, and marriage to the princess Goldeboru lead to the recovery of the thrones of Denmark and England. Its sympathetic depiction of labouring life and its Lincolnshire topography make it unique among the romances.
plot_or_argument: The orphaned Havelok is saved from the usurper Godard by the fisherman Grim, who flees with him to England; in disguise he serves as a kitchen hand at Lincoln, where the usurper Godrich marries the princess Goldeboru to him in mockery; Havelok's revealed royalty, his defeat of the usurpers, and his double coronation conclude the poem.
narrative_structure: A double exile-and-restoration plot (Havelok and Goldeboru in parallel), with an interpolated miracle episode and a long climactic battle.
principal_characters: Havelok; Goldeboru; Grim the fisherman; Godard; Godrich; Ubbe
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with marked northern (East Midland/Lincolnshire) dialect features.
historical_context: Composed c. 1280–90 in Lincolnshire, drawing on local legend (Grimsby's foundation) and Anglo-Norman sources (Lai d'Haveloc, Gaimar); preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108.
literary_significance: One of the finest English romances: its realism about work and poverty, and its fusion of folk-tale, dynastic, and hagiographical elements, make it a classic of the genre.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Laud Misc. 108. Standard edition: G. V. Smithers (1987).

title: Floris and Blancheflour
description: An idyllic romance of young love, adapted from the Old French Floire et Blancheflor: the Saracen prince Floris and the Christian captive Blancheflour, brought up together, are parted by his parents, and Floris pursues her to the emir's tower in Babylon, where love and loyalty overcome jealousy and force. The gentlest of the early English romances.
plot_or_argument: Floris's parents sell Blancheflour to merchants to end the match; she is taken to the emir of Babylon's harem tower; Floris follows, bribes his way in, is discovered in the maidens' tower, and is saved from death when the lovers' mutual devotion moves the emir to mercy and their marriage.
narrative_structure: A quest-romance in two movements (parting; pursuit and rescue), with the tower and the garden as symbolic settings.
principal_characters: Floris; Blancheflour; the emir of Babylon; Clarice; Darys the porter
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets, gently lyrical in tone.
historical_context: Composed c. 1250 in the south-east from the French Floire et Blancheflor (c. 1150), one of the most widely translated romances of the Middle Ages; preserved in four English manuscripts from c. 1300 onward.
literary_significance: The classic English romance of young love and constancy, and a key witness to the transmission of the sentimental romance from France to England.
bibliographical_notes: BL Egerton MS 2862; Cambridge, Gonville and Caius MS 175; etc. Standard edition: in Sentimental and Humorous Romances, TEAMS (2005).

title: Sir Orfeo
description: The masterpiece of the English Breton lay: the classical myth of Orpheus and Eurydice retold as a Celtic fairy romance, in which King Orfeo, harper of Winchester, loses his queen Heurodis to the fairy king and wins her back through the power of his music. Some 600 lines of haunting narrative, preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
plot_or_argument: Heurodis is taken by the fairy king from under the ympe-tree; Orfeo abandons his throne to live as a harper in the wilderness, sees his queen among the fairy riders, follows them into their castle, and recovers her by his harping; the poem ends with the steward's loyalty tested and the kingdom restored.
narrative_structure: A lai of loss, wilderness exile, and recovery, framed by the steward episode; the Otherworld journey is its centre.
principal_characters: Orfeo; Heurodis; the fairy king; the steward
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with lyrical set-pieces; economical and evocative.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in the London area, reworking the Orpheus myth through Celtic fairy-lore and the Breton lai tradition; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and two fifteenth-century copies.
literary_significance: Universally regarded as the finest of the Middle English Breton lays and one of the great short narratives of the period; the classical myth's medieval transformation is a touchstone of romance criticism.
bibliographical_notes: National Library of Scotland, Advocates' MS 19.2.1 (Auchinleck); BL Harley MS 3810; Ashmole 61. Standard editions: in A Book of Middle English; A. Laskaya and E. Salisbury, TEAMS (1995).

title: Amis and Amiloun
description: A romance of sworn brotherhood and sacrifice, adapted from the widespread European legend of the two friends: Amis and Amiloun, identical in appearance, exchange places in trial by combat and marriage, and Amis slays his own children to cure his friend's leprosy — before a miraculous restoration rewards their loyalty. One of the most powerful of the Auchinleck romances.
plot_or_argument: The sworn brothers part; Amiloun takes Amis's place in a judicial combat over a false accusation, and later, when Amiloun is struck with leprosy for the deception, Amis learns in a vision that his children's blood will cure him — and the sacrifice, made in secret, is rewarded by the children's resurrection.
narrative_structure: A double-plot of symmetrical substitution (combat; wedding-night; sacrifice), resolved by miracle and final reunion.
principal_characters: Amis; Amiloun; Belisaunt; the steward (villain); Amiloun's wife
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets in the Auchinleck manner.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman source (Ami et Amile), in the East Midlands; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and three later copies.
literary_significance: The classic English treatment of the friendship-and-sacrifice legend, and a favourite test case for the romance's religious and ethical codes.
bibliographical_notes: Auchinleck MS; BL Egerton MS 2862. Standard edition: in Amis and Amiloun, Robert of Cisyle, and Sir Amadace, TEAMS (1997).

title: Bevis of Hampton
description: One of the most popular of all Middle English romances: the adventures of Bevis of Southampton, sold into heathen lands by his mother's treachery, who wins the Saracen princess Josian, fights dragons and giants, and at last reclaims his English inheritance. Its vigorous, episodic narrative survived in verse, prose, and print into the seventeenth century.
plot_or_argument: Bevis's mother plots his father's murder and marries the murderer; the boy is sold overseas, but wins fame and the love of Josian; after adventures in Armenia, Cologne, and England — including his defeat of the dragon of Cologne and his final siege of Southampton — he regains his lands and ends his days as a monk with Josian.
narrative_structure: A sprawling episodic quest in the Auchinleck manner, with exile, conversion, combat, and restoration as its repeating units.
principal_characters: Bevis; Josian; Ascopard the giant; Saber; the dragon of Cologne; King Ermin
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets, later rewritten in tail-rhyme in some manuscripts.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman original (Boeve de Haumtoun); preserved in six manuscripts, the Auchinleck (c. 1330) foremost, and repeatedly printed from c. 1500 to the seventeenth century.
literary_significance: The archetypal popular romance: its immense circulation (Chaucer's Sir Thopas parodies its tail-rhyme form) makes it central to the history of English popular reading.
bibliographical_notes: Auchinleck MS; five other manuscripts. Standard edition: J. Fellows, in Four Romances of England, TEAMS (1999).

title: Guy of Warwick
alternative_titles: The Romance of Guy of Warwick
description: The longest and one of the most widely read of the English romances, in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas: the career of Guy, earl of Warwick, who wins the lady Felice by feats of arms, then renounces the world to fight as God's champion and die as a hermit. Its hero was England's favourite romance champion for three centuries.
plot_or_argument: Guy, a steward's son, wins Felice through tournaments and foreign wars; struck by remorse, he leaves her to do penance as a pilgrim, returning in disguise to defend England against the giant Colbrond at Winchester; recognized only at his death, he is buried by Felice, who follows him in holiness.
narrative_structure: A two-part structure — chivalric career, then penitential career — with the Colbrond episode and the deathbed recognition as climaxes.
principal_characters: Guy; Felice; Colbrond the giant; Reinbrun (their son); Herhaud
literary_form: romance in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas
meter_and_prosody: Couplets in the Auchinleck version; tail-rhyme stanzas in later copies.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300 from Anglo-Norman sources, drawing on Warwick legend and the cult of Guy; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript and many later copies and prints, into the seventeenth century.
literary_significance: The romance of Guy fixed the image of the penitent knight in English culture and remained a bestseller until the Civil War; it is central to the study of romance readership.
bibliographical_notes: Auchinleck MS; Cambridge, Gonville and Caius MS 107; etc. Standard edition: A. Mills, in Four Romances of England, TEAMS (1999).

title: Sir Launfal
description: Thomas Chestre's late fourteenth-century Breton lay of the fairy mistress: the knight Launfal, impoverished and slighted at Arthur's court, receives boundless wealth and the love of the fairy lady Tryamour on condition of secrecy, and is saved from death by her at his trial. The most accomplished English version of Marie de France's Lanval.
plot_or_argument: Launfal, neglected by Arthur, rides out in despair and meets Tryamour, whose gifts restore his magnificence; his boast of her beauty at court — provoked by the queen's advances — brings trial for treason, but Tryamour appears at the judgement, vindicates him, and carries him to the fairy isle of Olyroun.
narrative_structure: The classic lai structure: courtly exclusion, otherworld encounter, transgression, trial, and translation to the otherworld.
principal_characters: Launfal; Tryamour; Arthur; Guinevere (unnamed queen); the mayor of Caerleon
meter_and_prosody: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas of the popular romance kind.
historical_context: Composed c. 1390 by Thomas Chestre (who names himself in the poem), reworking the earlier Sir Landevale and Marie de France; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
literary_significance: The finest English fairy-mistress lay and the standard version of the Lanval story in English; a key text for the romance's treatment of women and power.
attribution_notes: The author names himself 'Thomas Chestre' in the poem's opening lines.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii. Standard edition: in The Middle English Breton Lays, TEAMS (1995).

title: Ywain and Gawain
description: The northern English adaptation of Chrétien de Troyes's Yvain: the knight Ywain wins Laudine by slaying her husband at the magic fountain, loses her by overstaying his leave, and regains her through madness, penance, and a career of championing the oppressed, with his lion as companion. The most accomplished English Arthurian romance after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
plot_or_argument: Ywain kills the fountain's defender and marries the widow Laudine through her maid Lunet's advocacy; forgetting his year's leave, he is rejected, goes mad, and is healed; as the Knight of the Lion he rights a succession of wrongs (the giant Harpin, the sisters' inheritance), and by keeping faith at last wins back Laudine.
narrative_structure: A quest-sequence of episodes bound by the fountain, the lion, and the promises made and broken, in the interlaced manner of French romance simplified for English taste.
principal_characters: Ywain; Laudine; Lunet; Gawain; the lion; the giant Harpin
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect.
historical_context: Composed c. 1325–50 in the north of England from Chrétien's Yvain (with an intermediary version); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Galba E.ix (c. 1400).
literary_significance: The chief English witness to the French Arthurian romance's central themes of love, honour, and self-knowledge, and a bridge between continental romance and Malory.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Galba E.ix. Standard edition: in Ywain and Gawain, Sir Percyvell of Gales, The Anturs of Arther, TEAMS (1995).

title: The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle
alternative_titles: The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell
description: A fifteenth-century Arthurian romance on the loathly lady theme: to save Arthur's life, Gawain marries the hideous Dame Ragnelle, who holds the answer to the riddle 'what women most desire' — sovereignty — and his courtesy at the wedding night transforms her into a beauty. The wittiest of the Gawain romances and the source of the Wife of Bath's Tale's plot.
plot_or_argument: Arthur, challenged by Sir Gromer Somer Joure, must learn what women most desire; Ragnelle supplies the answer (sovereignty) in exchange for Gawain's hand; Gawain's free gift of choice on the wedding night breaks the enchantment, making Ragnelle fair by day and night, and the two live happily until her death.
narrative_structure: A riddle-romance in two movements (the quest for the answer; the marriage and its testing), resolved by the courtesy test.
principal_characters: Gawain; Dame Ragnelle; Arthur; Sir Gromer Somer Joure
meter_and_prosody: Six-line tail-rhyme stanzas with comic energy.
historical_context: Composed c. 1450 in the East Midlands; preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Rawlinson MS C.86 (c. 1500); the loathly lady plot derives from Irish and English folk tradition (and parallels Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale).
literary_significance: The most entertaining of the late Gawain romances and the fullest English statement of the 'sovereignty' motif central to late medieval debates on marriage.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Rawlinson C.86. Standard edition: in Sir Gawain: Eleven Romances and Tales, TEAMS (1995).

title: Sir Degaré
description: A Breton lay of the foundling knight: Degaré, son of a fairy knight who ravished his mother, is exposed at birth, raised by a hermit, and wins his spurs through combat with a dragon; his search for his father ends in recognition, reunion, and the marriage of his widowed mother to her long-lost lover. Preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
plot_or_argument: Degaré, given his father's broken sword at birth, defeats the dragon, unhorses the knights of Arthur's court, and proves himself; seeking his father, he jousts with the fairy knight himself, and the two recognize each other; the poem ends with the father's return and the family's reunion.
narrative_structure: A foundling-quest in the lai manner, with the father-son combat as its climactic recognition scene.
principal_characters: Degaré; the fairy knight (his father); his mother; the hermit
historical_context: Composed c. 1325, probably in the south-east; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and later copies including the Percy Folio.
literary_significance: A representative minor lai valuable for the incest-anxieties and recognition patterns of the genre, and a staple of romance anthologies.
bibliographical_notes: Auchinleck MS; Bodleian Rawlinson Poetry 34. Standard edition: in The Middle English Breton Lays, TEAMS (1995).

title: Emaré
description: A Breton lay on the Constance legend: the princess Emaré, cast out by her incestuous father, drifts across the sea in a boat with her child, and through the marvellous cloth she weaves and the recognitions it brings, is restored to her husband and kingdom. The legend Chaucer used for the Man of Law's Tale, told as a fairy-tale of patient suffering.
plot_or_argument: Emaré, given a magic cloth by the emperor, refuses her father's marriage proposal and is set adrift; she marries the king of Galys, is slandered by her wicked mother-in-law and cast out again with her son Segramour; after years in Rome, her husband finds her and all are reconciled.
narrative_structure: A double exile-and-return plot organized by the magic cloth and the repeated sea voyages, in the Constance tradition.
principal_characters: Emaré; her father the emperor; the king of Galys; the wicked mother-in-law; Segramour
historical_context: Composed c. 1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, from the Constance legend (ultimately Trivet's chronicle, as in Chaucer); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
literary_significance: The most artful English version of the Constance story and a central text for the romance's treatment of incest, exile, and female patience.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii. Standard edition: in The Middle English Breton Lays, TEAMS (1995).

title: Athelston
description: A dark romance of kingship and treason, unique in the canon: the king Athelston, swayed by the traitor Wymond, puts his sworn brother and his family to the ordeal of fire, and is saved from tyranny only by the intervention of the archbishop and the test of the fire itself. Its grim political realism makes it unlike any other English romance.
plot_or_argument: Four messengers become sworn brothers; Athelston becomes king, and the envious Wymond persuades him that Earl Egeland plots treason; Athelston's violence against the earl's pregnant wife and children is halted when the archbishop curses him and the ordeal of fire acquits the innocent, exposing Wymond and restoring the fellowship.
narrative_structure: A compact tragedy of misrule in three movements (oath, slander, ordeal), with the archbishop's excommunication as its pivot.
principal_characters: Athelston; Wymond; Egeland; Edyff; the archbishop
meter_and_prosody: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, often grimly emphatic.
historical_context: Composed c. 1355–80 in the East Midlands, drawing on the legend of St Edmund and on baronial and ecclesiastical politics; preserved uniquely in Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 175.
literary_significance: The most politically serious of the English romances — a study of tyranny, sanctuary, and the ordeal — and a favourite text for the romance's engagement with law and kingship.
bibliographical_notes: Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, MS 175. Standard edition: in Amis and Amiloun, Robert of Cisyle, and Sir Amadace, TEAMS (1997).

title: Lancelot of the Laik
description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
plot_or_argument: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
narrative_structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
historical_context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
literary_significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
bibliographical_notes: Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5. Standard edition: W. W. Skeat, EETS OS 6 (1865).
